rows.question: What is the main claim of this piece, and where is it argued?
rows.text:
The piece's central claim is that it can be proven most published research findings are false, stated directly near the start [spya-xpu5tw] and restated in the section heading that follows it [spya-zjrg6r].

The argument runs in two stages. First, a mathematical model: the probability a claimed finding is actually true (the "positive predictive value") depends on the study's statistical power, its significance threshold, and the pre-study odds that the relationship being tested is real rather than nonexistent; the formula derived from a 2×2 table of true versus false relationships is laid out where the PPV equation is first given [spya-hjja9x]. Second, the model is extended to show that bias (design, analysis, and reporting choices that manufacture positive results) and competition among many research teams chasing the same question both push PPV down further [spya-gfvava spya-j7femp spya-zjre9m].

From that model the piece draws six corollaries — smaller studies, smaller effect sizes, more and less-selected tested relationships, more flexible designs, stronger financial/other interests, and "hotter" fields with more competing teams — each of which lowers the chance a finding is true [spya-nx5jjr spya-vzv8aq spya-p2upz7 spya-f65pfg spya-hkh8ey spya-s4b0q7 spya-mgrr58]. It then uses simulations across typical study types to argue that a positive predictive value above 50% is hard to achieve in most real research settings [spya-j5xgg2 spya-umhdpk], and closes by arguing that in fields with no true effects at all, "findings" simply measure the field's prevailing bias [spya-pw5xz4 spya-khfp04].

rows.question: What does the paragraph beginning “Corollary 1: The smaller the studies conducted in a scientific” mean?
rows.text:
That paragraph argues that research from small studies is less likely to be true than research from large studies, because small sample size reduces statistical power — the ability of a study to detect a real effect if one exists — and lower power pulls the proportion of true findings down toward the error-rate threshold. It gives an example: findings are more likely true in fields that run large studies, like heart-disease drug trials with several thousand patients, than in fields that typically run much smaller studies, like research looking for molecular markers that predict disease, where sample sizes can be around 100 times smaller [spya-vzv8aq].

This is the first of the six corollaries the author draws from the mathematical model set out earlier in the piece, where the chance a claimed finding is actually true (he calls this the positive predictive value) was shown to rise and fall with study power [spya-hjja9x spya-s46ctb]. Corollary 1 is just that relationship applied to the practical case of study size, since smaller samples generally mean lower power.

rows.question: Which paragraph gives the strongest support for the central claim, going only on the piece itself?
rows.text:
The paragraph under "Most Research Findings Are False for Most Research Designs and for Most Fields" does the most direct work: it says In the described framework, a PPV exceeding 50% is quite difficult to get. It then runs the simulation across concrete, representative research situations — a well-powered randomized trial, a confirmatory meta-analysis, early-phase trials, exploratory epidemiology, and mass-testing discovery research — and shows most of them land well under 50% true, e.g. Research findings from underpowered, early-phase clinical trials would be true about one in four times, or even less frequently if bias is present and even well-powered epidemiological studies may have only a one in five chance being true, if R = 1:10 [spya-umhdpk].

This is the strongest support because it's where the earlier algebra (the PPV formulas in spya-hjja9x, spya-s46ctb, and spya-u5x4p2) gets cashed out against the actual mix of study types in biomedical research, turning an abstract inequality into the title's concrete claim. The algebra alone only shows a finding is false under certain conditions on power, bias, and prior odds; this paragraph is where the piece argues those conditions are the normal case across most of the field, which is what "most published research findings are false" actually requires.

My inference is that the Box 1 worked example [spya-c5mfye spya-y0a3ah spya-uvmvbc] is a close second, since it makes the same point with one vivid numerical case, but it's a single illustrative scenario rather than the general sweep this paragraph makes.

rows.question: What does the author mean by positive predictive value?
rows.text:
The article defines positive predictive value (PPV) as the probability that a claimed research finding — one that reached statistical significance — is actually true, once the study is done [spya-hjja9x]. It is the "post-study probability" that a result is true, as opposed to the "pre-study probability" (how likely the relationship was to be true before any testing) [spya-hjja9x]. The author also notes that PPV is the complement of what another paper calls the "false positive report probability" [spya-hjja9x].

The piece gives a formula for PPV in terms of statistical power (1 − β), the significance threshold (α), and R, the ratio of true to false relationships being tested in a field: PPV = (1 − β)R / (R − βR + α) [spya-hjja9x]. Later sections extend this formula to account for bias and for multiple independent teams testing the same question, showing how PPV drops further under those conditions [spya-gfvava spya-s46ctb spya-zjre9m].

The argument runs in stages:

1. A mathematical framework defines the "positive predictive value" (PPV) — the chance a statistically significant finding is actually true — in terms of study power, significance threshold, and the pre-study ratio of true to false relationships being tested in a field [spya-hjja9x].
2. This framework is then extended to include bias (design, analysis, and reporting choices that manufacture "findings") and the effect of many independent teams testing the same question, both of which push PPV down further [spya-s46ctb spya-zjre9m].

rows.question: What is the main claim of this piece, and where is it argued?
rows.text:
The main claim is that people reason badly about anything that has become tied to their sense of self, so the best strategy for clear thinking is to minimize how many things you let into your identity. Graham states this directly: "If people can't think clearly about anything that has become part of their identity, then all other things being equal, the best plan is to let as few things into your identity as possible" [spya-xv45wq].

The argument builds up to that point in stages:

- He opens with the puzzle of why religion and politics produce bad discussions, and rules out "no right answer" as the explanation, noting "there are certainly some political questions that have definite answers, like how much a new government policy will cost. But the more precise political questions suffer the same fate as the vaguer ones" [spya-gv44uj].
- He locates the real cause in identity rather than topic, using the example that "a discussion today about a battle that took place in the Bronze Age probably wouldn't" degenerate into a fight, because "No one would know what side to be on" [spya-uz3ta2].
- He generalizes this with the programming-languages example, arguing the topic itself isn't unanswerable — identity just makes it feel that way [spya-s6tp4k].
- From there he draws the general rule that a topic can be discussed fruitfully only if it doesn't engage anyone's identity [spya-zdmhnz], which sets up the closing claim above.
- The final section narrows this into advice: don't just tolerate other views, don't even label yourself at all, since "The more labels you have for yourself, the dumber they make you" [spya-nt9xpg], with a carve-out in the notes for "scientist" as a label that doesn't commit you to specific beliefs [spya-mz9mzj].

rows.question: What does the paragraph beginning “More generally, you can have a fruitful discussion about a” mean?
rows.text:
That paragraph generalizes the piece's core claim: a conversation can stay useful only if the topic doesn't touch any participant's sense of who they are. Politics and religion are especially dangerous not because of their subject matter but because they happen to be bound up with many people's self-image, while in principle you could discuss even those topics productively with someone who doesn't treat them as identity-stakes. Conversely, something as ordinary as which pickup truck brand is better can turn into the same kind of unproductive fight if it happens to be wrapped up in someone's identity [spya-zdmhnz].

My inference is that this paragraph is doing the pivot in the essay's argument: the earlier paragraphs use religion and politics as examples, and this one strips the examples away to state the general rule — it's identity-engagement, not topic, that ruins discussions — which then sets up the final move into the essay's advice about keeping your own identity small [spya-xv45wq].
